The Doppler shift depends on the component of the relative velocity of source and detector **along the line joining them**.  
- In (A) the source approaches the detector, so the distance between them decreases → a shift.  
- In (B) the detector approaches the source, again a decreasing distance → a shift.  
- In (D) they move away from each other, the distance increases → a shift.  

Only in (C) can the relative radial velocity be zero. If the source and detector travel in the same direction **with the same speed** (or, more generally, if their motion has no component along the line joining them), the distance between them stays constant, so the detector receives the wavefronts at the same rate they are emitted. Hence no Doppler shift is possible.

**Final answer: C**
